If the user's ISP does happen to block port 8333, there are a few solutions they can turn to, all of which require a little bit of effort and technical ability on the end users part.

For starters, users can ask their ISP’s to put the router into “Bridge Mode”. This turns the ISPs hardware into nothing more than a simple connection to the Internet. The user would be required to provide their own router, and to handle the configuration and maintenance of that hardware. The downside is that many ISPs limit technical support when a home user requests their router be put into Bridge Mode.

A second option, very similar to Bridge Mode, is to get a business account with the ISP. While these typically cost more money per month, they do come with additional benefits such as static IP Addresses, and higher bandwidth. Depending on the provider, business account may or may not come with their own Router, so users must be prepared to manage their own hardware with this scenario as well.

If users are concerned with telling their ISPs that they’re running a Bitcoin client, it just so happens that a few other well known services use port 8333. Instead of revealing any information about Bitcoin, users may tell their ISPs they’re running the VMWare Server Management User Interface, or the Y-Cam Wireless IP Camera.

You seem to have misunderstood UEFI. It's a different and honestly better alternative to BIOS (more info for guest OSes, faster boot times, compatibility with GPT partition tables...) -- it isn't a Microsoft thing (Apple's been using UEFI since...at least 2010 if memory serves). It doesn't naturally restrict what kernels can be run. That's an optional feature called "secure boot."

You can turn off secure boot, which is the only reason you'd need a Microsoft signed kernel. Secure boot is just showboating anyway, and so I wouldn't quibble over it. Just build in SELinux if you're so interested in a secure kernel.

Linux has native UEFI support and also supports stubbing. There's no problem there. I run a custom kernel on a Yoga 2 Pro from Lenovo. You just have to include the UEFI option when you configure it.

UEFI doesn't have any intrinsic problems booting into Linux. Matter of fact, it's a faster than standard BIOSes. As long as you have a modern Linux distro's live media, you just boot into it through UEFI (not legacy BIOS) and install the system. On a more advanced system, just install grub2, gummiboot or whatever bootloader you like, provided that it has UEFI support, and it'll be fine. If you're having to boot through legacy you either a) downloaded the wrong ISO, b) are trying to use a deprecated Linux distro, or c) didn't make sure your checksums were in order.

So, no, you don't need a "UEFI off switch," you just have to disable secure boot and then do your shit like normal. For advanced users, after you've installed and configured, it is possible to re-enable secure boot. I agree that secure boot should be more open, but that's irrelevant given that we can simply turn it off.

http://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2015/03/windows-10-to-make-the-secure-boot-alt-os-lock-out-a-reality/

While I admit I have used the nomenclature incorrectly (and you are correct; I will keep this in mind in the future and try to be more accurate), the secure boot feature still no longer requires an off switch with Windows 10, and explicitly omits it for tablets.

My concern, however, is not in the security of a kernel, nor the UEFI firmware by itself in terms of provided system services. My concern is whether or not someone can boot on a machine with secure boot enabled, and be able to use their own compiled and configured kernel (or boot loader, for that matter). To the best of my knowledge, your options are to use a pre-signed kernel from a major distribution, or to use a boot shim, and both of these approaches have drawbacks; in particular I recall that the pre-signed kernels are not allowed to include unsigned binary modules (e.g. graphics drivers), and this is obviously a problem for compiling your own kernel. Obviously these are not good if you can't turn off secure boot. Is this the case? Are there workarounds for this that I am unaware of? And if it works for Linux, will it work for other alternative operating systems such as BSD?

I hadn't heard of the new Windows 10 boot lock, but it doesn't surprise me all that much. I'm not aware of other methods, although a well-done shim should be fine, if a bit tedious to maintain.

Given this development, I would expect that coreboot and similar free software alternatives to UEFI/BIOS will see more extensive development. If it does, we'll probably have to start flashing our devices with free UEFI alternatives.
